items.summary: Supreme Court Justice Ujjal Bhuyan on Sunday said that any process which disenfranchises millions of Indian citizens is intrinsically arbitrary and a negation of the constitutional order. No whataboutery can justify the act of taking away voting rights of citizens, he criticised. "If any process results in disenfranchising millions and millions of Indian citizens making them second class citizens in their own country in the sense of being citizens without voting rights, such a process is intrinsically arbitrary. No amount of whataboutery can justify it. It strikes at the very heart of the Constitution and I would go to the extent of saying that it is a negation of the constitutional order which we have adopted under the Constitution of India," he said. Justice Bhuyan was delivering the valedictory address at the 19th NALSAR-Justice BR Sawhney Memorial Moot Court Competition at NALSAR University of Law, Hyderabad. "Indian Constitution does not provide for two classes of citizens: citizens with voting rights and citizens without voting rights. Any process which leads to wholesale disenfranchisement of Indian citizens making them citizens without voting rights would be violative of Articles 326 and 14 of the Constitution of India," he said. He made clear that no institution was exempt. "No authority can do it; no court can condone it. No one is above the Constitution," he declared. On the deletion of names from electoral rolls, Justice Bhuyan was categorical. "Except in the case of a dead voter, the name of a voter once enlisted in the electoral roll cannot be deleted without notice and hearing. However, returning the power of judicial appointment to the government would severely compromise the independence of the judiciary, he warned. “Now there are lots of pot shots being thrown at the Collegium system today rightly. If anybody can devise a better system of appointment, I am all for it (but) certainly not reversion to government, no way,” Justice Nariman said. He also criticised the 103rd Constitutional Amendment, arguing that extending economic reservations to upper castes turns constitutional principles on their head. He warned that India’s constitutional institutions are currently experiencing a great decline. “The institutions today that the Constitution has laid down are unfortunately in great decline," Justice Nariman said. Collegium system Justice Nariman acknowledged valid criticisms surrounding judicial appointments. However, he firmly cautioned against restoring executive control over the appointment process. To make his point, he flagged the current state of the Election Commission of India (ECI). “We have seen what damage government has already done to the Election Commission an extremely important thing which is at the heart of our democracy,” the judge said. items.title: Right to vote in great peril: Justice Rohinton Nariman flags executive interference in Election Commission
items.summary: Former Supreme Court Justice Rohinton Nariman has expressed grave concern over the functioning of the Election Commission of India (ECI), particularly large scale voter exclusion and executive interference in appointments to the electoral body. In a speech delivered on September 27, Justice warned that the citizens's right to vote is facing unprecedented threats. “The common man today under our Constitution, and if I may say so, the heart of our Constitution, the heart of our democracy, which is the right to vote, is in great peril,” Justice Nariman stated. He pointed out that an astounding number of 90 lakh were disenfranchised. 22 lakh affected citizens filed appeals against the ECI decision, and among the 1 lakh appeals decided, an overwhelming 93 percent verdicts eventually came in favour of the excluded, he said. “So can you imagine, this was a completely illegal knocking out of the common man, of the citizen of India, in order that a government obtains what it wants. And the result of that you saw in West Bengal was something that upset the government of the day and brought in the government of the centre,” he said. He was speaking at the Centenary Oration on ‘The Constitution and the Common Man Justice Rohinton Nariman The heart democracy, which is the right to vote, is in great peril. Justice Nariman was also critical of legislative changes governing the selection of Election Commissioners in 2023. He referred to the order in the Anoop Baranwal case where the Supreme Court recommended a neutral selection panel comprising the Prime Minister, the Leader of the Opposition and the Chief Justice of India. However, the parliament replaced the Chief Justice with a Union Cabinet Minister, effectively restoring executive dominance over appointments. “So that again, you are back to square one,” he remarked. He urged the apex court to intervene urgently to rectify the situation and safeguard the integrity of elections. He referred to reports by Indian Express that Election Commissioners Sukhbir Singh Sandhu and Vivek Joshi had objected to the decisions taken by the Chief Election Commissioner (CEC) on 14 occasions. Justice Nariman emphasised that the Supreme Court must ensure a balanced selection mechanism to preserve public trust. “I hope that the apex court, an institution to which I once belonged, steps in immediately and rectifies these things. items.title: Owaisi says Hyderabad will see massive protests if ECI doesn’t act on Form 7 misuse
items.summary: Follow TNM's WhatsApp channel for news updates and story links. Hyderabad MP and All India Majlis-e-Ittehadul Muslimeen (AIMIM) chief Asaduddin Owaisi said that Hyderabad would witness massive protests if the Election Commission of India (ECI) does not act against those who are allegedly seeking the deletion of genuine Muslim voters from the electoral rolls by filing Form 7s, citing false reasons. “We cannot tolerate if despite being genuine voters, people’s names are sought to be deleted from electoral rolls through Form 7 just for being Muslim. If ECI looks the other way, allowing BJP members to strike out names of Muslim voters, we will not let that happen,” Owaisi said, while addressing a gathering at the Jalsa-e-Milad-un-Nabi event on Saturday, October 3, at the Milad Maidan near Golconda. Owaisi made the above remarks soon after an incident of alleged misuse of Form 7 came to light from Hyderabad. Around 30 Muslim voters at a polling station in Musheerabad constituency had to face an inquiry from Election Commission officials after their neighbour SV Balachander, also the booth level agent (BLA) of the Bharatiya Janata Party (BJP) for their polling station, filed Form 7 objections to their names being included in the electoral roll. Balachander allegedly claimed that the voters, including the family members of Congress BLA and the party’s Bagh Lingampally division vice president Mohammad Baba Sharfuddin, had duplicate votes. Sharfuddin told TNM that when he confronted Balachander, he said he didn’t even know what a Form 7 was, and that he had signed and submitted pre-printed forms based on instructions from his party office. View this post on Instagram “If false Form 7 forms are being filed, we appeal to the Election Commission to take action against those responsible. If this drama does not stop, remember, protests bigger than those at Delhi’s Jantar Mantar will take place on the roads and streets of Hyderabad, and it will create a lot of trouble for you,” Owaisi said. Form 7 is used to object to the inclusion of a name in the electoral roll or to seek its deletion for reasons such as the person having died, absent or permanently shifted from their residence, being already enrolled in the electoral rolls elsewhere, being under 18 years of age, or not being an Indian citizen. It compared the protests to the 2024 Gen Z revolution in Bangladesh that led to the ouster of then Prime Minister Sheikh Hasina. In an article titled ‘ECI controversy resembles Bangladesh regime change playbook; Is it a CIA conspiracy to destabilise India?’, the magazine posed the question without citing any source or document. It asked whether the ongoing protests against SIR were the “first step in the larger plot weaved by the hidden hands”. Organiser claimed that the allegations of irregularities and a fractured consensus in the ECI revisit a pattern seen in Bangladesh. It claimed that “intelligence sources” and “geopolitical analysts” believe that the CIA targeted Bangladesh’s Election Commission first. According to the article, CEC KM Nurul Huda was “pitched against” Election Commissioner Mahbub Talukdar. It says news of this rift spread rapidly and fuelled public distrust. This, it claims, led to the student uprising that toppled the Awami League government, while providing no supporting evidence. The Bangladesh protests began in June 2024 over a quota that reserved 30% of government jobs for descendants of 1971 Liberation War veterans. Students demanded a merit-based system, but the government’s crackdown transformed the movement into a broader anti-government uprising. Authorities cut internet access, imposed a curfew and deployed security forces as clashes intensified. The Supreme Court later reduced the veterans’ quota to 5%, but protests continued amid demands for accountability for those killed. items.title: Heat, lost income, and violence: How Chennai women are bearing the cost of a hotter city
items.summary: The kathrikka (brinjal) curry was bubbling in a large aluminium pot, sending up the smell of fried onions and spices into the narrow lane outside Kalaivani’s one-room home. She chopped another handful of onions, stirred the curry, and checked the flame, moving between the chores without pausing. Around her, dirty water trickled through the lane. A few metres away, tiny, dark rooms that stored animal hides filled the air with a heavy stench. Further ahead stood a large cattle shed, where women worked on the hides left behind after slaughter. This is Puliyanthope in North Chennai, where generations of families, many of them Dalit and Muslim, live alongside slaughterhouses, tanneries, and the waste that comes with them. But for Kalaivani, the hardest part of living here is not the filth or the stench. It is the heat. “In summer, it is not possible to go to work or sit at home. It is boiling hot inside my house. At night, I am not able to sleep properly. I wake up multiple times and pour water all over my body,” she said. By morning, she is exhausted. “The next day, I don’t even feel like getting up. Since I work for daily wages, I cannot afford to skip work,” she said. For Kalaivani, a domestic worker, there is no choice between resting and working, as missing a day’s work means losing that day’s income. Her husband drinks every day, she said. When he runs short of money, he asks her for some. If she refuses, he becomes angry. “At times, I lose control and shout back at him. With all this sleeplessness and pain, I am not always able to hold back,” she said. Then came the sentence that stayed in the room long after she had said it. “He hits me sometimes,” Kalaivani said, smiling apologetically, as though explaining something that was somehow her fault. Her mother Selvi interrupted. “Not sometimes. Whenever he is angry, he hits her,” Selvi said. The mother and daughter continued talking as life in the lane carried on around them. Cows nosed through plastic waste. Children moved through the narrow passage. For women like Kalaivani, the heat is not simply endured outdoors. It follows them from the workplace to the household, affecting their bodies, their incomes, and sometimes, their safety.
